forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

compliance.notes: Re-scored on BCP's complete 2026/27 pack after the capital and budget documents were supplied by hand; the earlier assessment_caveat is CLEARED (explicit "") because the capital-strategy content is now in evidence and the residual gaps are BCP's, not ours. BCP publishes no standalone capital strategy: its capital strategy is a section of the Cabinet budget report of 11 February 2026 (paras 66-82, 'The capital strategy is based on the following core principles'), with the Capital Investment Programme (Appendices 7 and 7a) and the 2026-2031 Strategic Asset Management Plan (Appendix 8) as its substance, all recommended to full Council (recommendations viii-x, unchanged by the 10 February addendum). STRONGEST: the liability benchmark (separate General Fund and HRA charts plotting all four balances to 2095); the capital expenditure / financing / CFR chain (five-year GF and HRA tables in the TMS, reconciled to a four-year programme by directorate and by scheme); the borrowing strategy and its candid handling of the projected over-borrowed position driven by cash-flowing the DSG/SEND deficit; the MRP policy (annuity asset-life, £12.8m of VRP overpayments disclosed); the creditworthiness policy (ratings plus a CDS overlay); and the S151 officer's s25 affordability and reserves advice. WEAKEST, and now confirmed as real gaps rather than missing documents: no financing-costs-to-net-revenue-stream ratio for either fund (PI-07), no upper/lower limits on the maturity structure of borrowing (PI-09) and no fixed/variable interest-rate exposure limits (RISK-02) — three core indicators absent from a 'Treasury Indicators' section that sets only the operational boundary and the authorised limit (and those as a single combined line, in a table headed £'000 whose figures are £m). On the commercial side the supplied capital documents confirm that BCP holds non-treasury investments (investment properties within a £2.16bn estate, council-owned companies and joint ventures, a £15.3m development exposure at Carters Quay) but nowhere quantifies them: no proportionality test against reserves (COM-03, core), no schedule of non-treasury investments by purpose (COM-04), no net commercial/service income ratio (PI-08) and no income-dependence or contingency disclosure (COM-07). Also absent: the promised specified/non-specified investment sections (INV-05), a portfolio risk-exposure indicator (INV-06), any derivatives policy (RISK-06) and any flag on audit qualification of the source data (RPT-05). The Treasury Management Policy, Practices and Schedules document (TMS para 82, 'will be presented alongside') is not in the pack, which limits TMP-01 and GOV-02 but nothing core.

gaps.evidence: TMS p.16 para 80 'The maximum period for investments will be 5 years'; p.15 para 75 sets time limits by counterparty type (local authorities 5 years, Banks 1 higher quality 2 years, Banks 1 medium quality 1 year, DMADF 6 months).
TMS p.10 para 59 reproduces the substance of Prudential Code para 51 and Budget report p.20 para 67 commits every borrowing-funded business case to the PWLB borrowing restrictions.

TMS p.24 Appendix 3: the S151 officer is responsible for 'ensuring the proportionality of all investments so that the Authority does not undertake a level of investing which exposes the Authority to an excessive level of risk compared to its financial resources'; TMS p.6 para 32 asks members, by approving the CFR figures, to 'consider the scale proportionate to the Council's remaining activity'; Budget report p.37 acknowledges exposure to council-owned companies and joint ventures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C3 - Officer Decision record CEO urgent decision seafront
findings.headline: Bournemouth Pier funding reduced from £9.57m to £7.50m as consequence of East Cliff prioritisation
findings.detail: The reallocation reduces Pier funding by £1.76m. The council acknowledges Bournemouth Pier remains a longer-term infrastructure challenge. The reduced allocation will now cover only removal of deteriorated landing stages and critical sub-structural repairs, while a longer-term investment strategy remains under consideration.
findings.matters: A second major seafront capital asset is now under-resourced relative to need, signalling the council has multiple material infrastructure challenges competing for limited capital and no resolved long-term funding strategy.
findings.figures: Original Pier allocation £9.57m; revised allocation £7.50m; reduction £1.76m
findings.quote: It is recognised that the reallocation reduces the funding available for works to Bournemouth Pier, which remains a longer-term infrastructure challenge for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C3 - Officer Decision record CEO urgent decision seafront
findings.headline: Council faces potential borrowing requirement if Levelling Up Fund is not deployed to urgent infrastructure need
findings.detail: The decision explicitly flags that if the Levelling Up Fund reallocation is not deployed, the council would need to fund essential cliff stabilisation works through borrowing or other financing arrangements. This would create additional revenue and budget pressures.
findings.matters: Contingent borrowing exposure signals that the council lacks sufficient capital resources for critical infrastructure maintenance, which would increase debt servicing costs and squeeze revenue budgets.
findings.figures: £1.76m reallocation; total LUF programme £19.99m; LUF expenditure deadline 31 March 2028
findings.quote: If this funding is not utilised, the Council may need to fund essential works through borrowing or other financing arrangements, creating additional revenue and budget pressures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C3 - Officer Decision record CEO urgent decision seafront
findings.headline: Exclusion zone from cliff instability restricting public access and reducing income generation
findings.detail: A substantial exclusion zone remains in place at East Cliff, restricting public access and limiting facility operations until permanent stabilisation works are completed. This directly impacts the council's ability to generate income from seafront services and create operational revenue.
findings.matters: Loss of operational income from council-operated or licensed seafront facilities weakens the council's revenue position and financial resilience.
findings.quote: A substantial exclusion zone remains in place, restricting public access, limiting the operation of key facilities and impacting income generation until permanent works can be completed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C3 - Officer Decision record CEO urgent decision seafront
findings.headline: East Cliff cliff stabilisation requires £1.76m emergency reallocation after two landslips in six years
findings.detail: East Cliff is one of the council's highest-risk seafront assets. After a significant landslip in 2016, the council allocated £4.31m for East Flank stabilisation. A further landslip occurred on the West Flank in 2024. A competitive tender process in 2025 returned four bids, with the lowest-priced tender exceeding the budget currently available, forcing the reallocation.
findings.matters: Material infrastructure asset failure with recurring defects directly affects the council's asset base, public safety liability, and financial stability.
findings.quote: A further landslip occurred on the West Flank in 2024, creating an additional requirement for major stabilisation works. A competitive tender process for stabilisation of both flanks was undertaken in 2025. Four compliant bids were received, with the lowest-priced tender exceeding the budget currently available.

findings.headline: Aggressive income maximization through fees, charges, grants and commercial activity
findings.detail: The council is pursuing income generation through fees and charges, grant opportunities, commercial activity, improved cost recovery, and strengthened collection rates across the organization.
findings.matters: Aggressive income pursuit combined with emergency spend controls indicates a significant funding gap being tackled from both sides; commercial activity and grant chasing in crisis mode suggest limited alternative funding.
findings.figures: Comprehensive income initiatives across multiple revenue streams (targets not stated)
findings.quote: Maximise income generation through fees and charges, grant opportunities, commercial activity, improved cost recovery and strengthened collection rates.
